questions.sec: Alport syndrome: collagen & type IV collagen table · p783
questions.q: Alport syndrome is also known as hereditary nephritis and is caused by a mutation in:
opts: Collagen IV (COL4A5), most commonly a deletion
Collagen III (COL3A1), most commonly a point mutation
Nephrin (NPHS1), most commonly a missense mutation
questions.exp: Alport syndrome = hereditary nephritis; the mutation is in collagen IV (COL4A5), with deletion as the commonest type. (Book p783)

questions.sec: Alport syndrome: collagen & type IV collagen table · p783
questions.q: Fill up: In Alport syndrome the commonest type of COL4A5 mutation is a ______.
questions.exp: Mutation in collagen IV (COL4A5): the commonest is a deletion. (Book p783)

questions.sec: Alport syndrome: collagen & type IV collagen table · p783
questions.q: Match each type IV collagen heterotrimer with the basement membrane in which it is seen — 1) α1–α1–α2  2) α3–α4–α5  3) α5–α5–α6 … A) GBM, cochlea and ocular BM  B) Seen from birth  C) Skin basement membrane
questions.exp: Type IV collagen table: α1-α1-α2 is seen from birth; α3-α4-α5 is found in the GBM, cochlea and ocular BM; α5-α5-α6 is found in skin basement membrane. (Book p783)

questions.sec: Alport syndrome: collagen & type IV collagen table · p783
questions.q: Alport syndrome damages the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea and ocular basement membrane but the skin basement membrane is spared in the classical form. Which collagen chain combination explains this distribution?
questions.exp: The α3-α4-α5 heterotrimer is seen in the GBM, cochlea and ocular BM — the three sites involved in Alport syndrome. α5-α5-α6 marks skin basement membrane. (Book p783)

questions.sec: Alport syndrome: collagen & type IV collagen table · p783
questions.q: The α1–α1–α2 collagen IV trimer is present in basement membranes from birth.
opts: True — the table lists it under 'seen in: birth'
False — it appears only after 30 years of age
False — it is confined to the skin basement membrane
True, but only in patients with Alport syndrome
questions.exp: The type IV collagen table lists α1-α1-α2 against 'birth'. (Book p783)

questions.sec: Alport syndrome: collagen & type IV collagen table · p783
questions.q: Which site is NOT listed as a location of the α3–α4–α5 collagen IV network?
questions.exp: α3-α4-α5 is seen in GBM, cochlea and ocular BM; skin basement membrane contains α5-α5-α6. (Book p783)

questions.q: Match the mode of inheritance with the affected chain in Alport syndrome — 1) X-linked (80%)  2) Autosomal recessive (15%)  3) Autosomal dominant (5%) … A) α3/α4  B) α5  C) α3/α4
questions.exp: Inheritance table: X-linked (80%) affects the α5 chain; AR (15%) and AD (5%) both affect α3/α4. (Book p783)

questions.q: The commonest mode of inheritance in Alport syndrome, X-linked, accounts for:
questions.exp: X-linked inheritance accounts for 80% of Alport syndrome, affecting the α5 chain, with ESRD by 30 years in males and females as carriers. (Book p783)

questions.q: A man with X-linked Alport syndrome reaches end-stage renal disease. According to the table, ESRD occurs:
questions.exp: X-linked (80%) Alport syndrome: ESRD by 30 years in males (♂), with females (♀) as carriers. (Book p783)

questions.q: In the AR form of Alport syndrome, ESRD occurs by 40 years and affects both females and males.
opts: False — AR Alport causes ESRD only in males by 30 years
False — AR Alport never causes ESRD
True, but AR accounts for 80% of cases
questions.exp: AR (15%) affects α3/α4 and causes ESRD by 40 years in both ♀ and ♂. (Book p783)

questions.q: Match the inheritance pattern with its typical severity — 1) X-linked Alport  2) AD Alport … A) Mild disease in both females and males  B) ESRD by 30 years in males, females are carriers
opts: Both cause ESRD by 30 years in females
questions.exp: X-linked: ESRD by 30 years in males, females carriers. AD (5%): mild disease in ♀ and ♂. (Book p783)

questions.q: Fill up: Autosomal dominant Alport syndrome (5%) produces ______ disease in females and males.
questions.exp: AD (5%) Alport syndrome affects α3/α4 and produces mild disease in both females and males. (Book p783)

questions.q: Autosomal recessive Alport syndrome accounts for what proportion of cases?
questions.exp: Alport inheritance: X-linked 80%, AR 15%, AD 5%. (Book p783)

questions.q: Match the timeline in Alport syndrome with the feature — 1) 5 years  2) 10 years  3) 10–15 years  4) 25–30 years … A) ESRD  B) Proteinuria + hypertension  C) Creatinine rises  D) Asymptomatic microhematuria
questions.exp: Timeline: 5 years asymptomatic microhaematuria; 10 years proteinuria + hypertension; 10–15 years rising creatinine; 25–30 years ESRD. (Book p783)

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy with a strong family history of renal failure has a rising serum creatinine. On the clinical-features table, at which point in the timeline does this occur?
questions.exp: The Alport timeline places 'creatinine ↑' at 10–15 years, after microhaematuria at 5 years and proteinuria with HTN at 10 years. (Book p783)

questions.q: The earliest renal manifestation in Alport syndrome (5 years) is asymptomatic microhematuria.
opts: False — the earliest feature is nephrotic-range proteinuria
False — the earliest feature is ESRD
True, but it begins only after 10 years
questions.exp: Timeline, 5 years: asymptomatic microhaematuria; proteinuria with hypertension appears only at 10 years. (Book p783)

questions.q: The ENT manifestation of Alport syndrome at 15 years is sensorineural hearing loss that characteristically begins at:
opts: Low frequency (the commonest pattern), then progresses to high frequency
High frequency (the commonest pattern), then progresses to low frequency
Sudden total deafness in the first year of life
questions.exp: ENT manifestation at 15 years: SNHL of low frequency (m/c) which subsequently becomes high frequency. (Book p783)

questions.q: Fill up: The hearing loss of Alport syndrome is sensorineural, abbreviated ______.
questions.exp: Alport syndrome produces SNHL (sensorineural hearing loss), initially low frequency, later high frequency. (Book p783)

questions.q: A 20-year-old man with Alport syndrome is examined at the slit lamp. The pathognomonic ocular sign is:
opts: Anterior lenticonus with an oil droplet appearance
questions.exp: Ocular manifestations at 20 years: anterior lenticonus (pathognomonic), with an oil droplet appearance on slit lamp. (Book p783)

questions.q: Fill up: The pathognomonic ocular manifestation of Alport syndrome is anterior ______.
questions.exp: Anterior lenticonus — marked pathognomonic in the table — with an oil droplet appearance on slit lamp at 20 years. (Book p783)

questions.q: The ocular findings described in Alport syndrome are an oil droplet appearance on slit lamp and anterior lenticonus.
opts: False — the described finding is a cherry-red spot
False — the described finding is a Kayser–Fleischer ring
True, but only in the AD form
questions.exp: Ocular manifestations at 20 years: anterior lenticonus (pathognomonic) and oil droplet appearance on slit lamp. (Book p783)

questions.q: All but one of the following appear in the Alport clinical-features timeline. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: The 5-year entry is asymptomatic microhaematuria; proteinuria (with HTN) appears at 10 years, and ESRD at 25–30 years. (Book p783)

questions.q: A patient with Alport syndrome presents at 27 years with uraemic symptoms — fitting the last row of the clinical-features table, which reads:
questions.exp: The final timeline row of the Alport table is ESRD at 25–30 years. (Book p783)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: Match each Alport investigation with its finding — 1) Light microscopy and immunofluorescence  2) Electron microscopy … A) Splitting + lamellation of lamina densa with alternating thick and thin foci  B) Normal
questions.exp: In Alport syndrome, LM and IF are normal, while EM shows splitting + lamellation of the lamina densa with alternating thick and thin foci (basket-weave appearance). (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: The electron-microscopy appearance described in Alport syndrome is:
opts: Splitting and lamellation of the lamina densa with a basket-weave appearance
Subepithelial camel-hump deposits with a starry sky pattern on IF
Intramembranous dense-body deposits with tram-track capillary duplication
Uniformly thin glomerular basement membrane without any lamellation
questions.exp: EM in Alport syndrome: splitting + lamellation of the lamina densa, alternating thick and thin foci, giving a basket-weave appearance. (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: Light microscopy and immunofluorescence are typically normal in Alport syndrome, the diagnosis resting on electron microscopy.
opts: False — LM shows crescents in all cases
False — IF shows linear IgG in all cases
True, but only in the autosomal dominant form
questions.exp: Investigation in Alport syndrome: LM and IF are normal; EM shows splitting/lamellation of the lamina densa with a basket-weave pattern. (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: The treatment given for Alport syndrome in the book is:
questions.exp: Rx in Alport syndrome: transplant — with the post-transplant complication of Goodpasture syndrome (antibody against α3). (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: What percentage of Alport patients develop Goodpasture syndrome as a complication after transplantation?
questions.exp: Complication post-transplant in Alport syndrome: 5% develop Goodpasture syndrome, from antibodies against α3 (collagen). (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: A man with Alport syndrome received a kidney transplant; 8 months later anti-GBM antibody is detected. Which explanation fits the book?
opts: Antibody against α3 collagen of the graft — post-transplant Goodpasture syndrome in 5%
Recurrence of Alport syndrome in the graft in 50%
Recurrent PSGN from a streptococcal throat infection
questions.exp: Alport syndrome post-transplant: 5% develop Goodpasture syndrome due to antibody against α3, because the native α3 had never been 'seen' by the immune system. (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: Thin GBM disease is inherited as and caused by:
questions.exp: Thin GBM disease: AD, COL4A4/A3 mutation. (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: Match thin GBM disease features with their descriptions — 1) Clinical features  2) Light microscopy and IF  3) Electron microscopy … A) Normal  B) Microscopic haematuria (<5 years) with good prognosis  C) Uniformly thin (<200–300 nm)
questions.exp: Thin GBM disease: microscopic haematuria (<5 years) with good prognosis; LM and IF normal; EM shows a uniformly thin GBM (<200–300 nm). (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: On electron microscopy, the glomerular basement membrane in thin GBM disease measures:
questions.exp: EM in thin GBM disease: uniformly thin GBM, <200–300 nm. (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: Thin GBM disease usually has a good prognosis, presenting with microscopic haematuria below 5 years of age.
opts: False — it progresses to ESRD by 30 years
False — it presents with nephrotic syndrome
questions.exp: Thin GBM disease clinical features: microscopic haematuria (<5 years) and good prognosis; LM/IF are normal with EM showing a uniformly thin GBM. (Book p784)

questions.sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784
questions.q: All but one of the following are seen in thin GBM disease. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Basket-weave splitting of the lamina densa
questions.exp: Basket-weave splitting/lamellation of the lamina densa belongs to Alport syndrome; thin GBM disease simply shows a uniformly thin GBM on EM. (Book p784)

questions.q: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disease caused by a defect in:
questions.exp: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disease caused by a defect in α-galactosidase. (Book p784)

questions.q: Match each Fabry feature with its description — 1) Angiokeratoma  2) Accumulation in vessels  3) Renal involvement … A) Heart, cerebrovascular and cornea verticillata  B) Appears in the 2nd decade  C) Asymptomatic microhaematuria + proteinuria, the earliest, with ESRD by the 4th–5th decade
questions.exp: Fabry features: acroparesthesia; angiokeratoma (2nd decade); accumulation in vessels of heart, cerebrovascular system and cornea verticillata; renal — asymptomatic microhaematuria + proteinuria (earliest) with ESRD by the 4th–5th decade. (Book p784)

questions.q: The earliest renal abnormality in Fabry disease is:
questions.exp: Renal involvement in Fabry disease: asymptomatic microhaematuria + proteinuria is the earliest, culminating in ESRD by the 4th–5th decade. (Book p784)

questions.q: In Fabry disease, ESRD develops by the:
questions.exp: Renal feature of Fabry disease: asymptomatic microhaematuria + proteinuria (earliest) with ESRD by the 4th–5th decade. (Book p784)

questions.q: Fill up: The skin lesion of Fabry disease shown in the figure is ______, appearing in the 2nd decade.
questions.exp: Fabry disease produces angiokeratoma (in the 2nd decade), shown in the accompanying figure. (Book p784)

questions.q: All but one of the following are listed as sites of vessel accumulation in Fabry disease. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Accumulation in vessels is described for heart, cerebrovascular system and cornea verticillata; the renal features are microhaematuria/proteinuria and podocyte vacuolation. (Book p784)

questions.q: A 32-year-old man has acroparesthesia, angiokeratomas over the bathing-trunk area and proteinuria. Urine microscopy under polarised light shows lipid deposits. Which investigation matches Fabry disease?
opts: Urine — maltese cross deposits under polarised light; biopsy — vacuolation of podocytes
Urine — hexagonal cystine crystals; biopsy — glomerular crescents
Urine — calcium oxalate crystals; biopsy — calcium deposits
Urine — oval fat bodies only; biopsy — normal glomeruli
questions.exp: Investigations in Fabry disease: urine shows maltese cross deposits under polarised light; renal biopsy shows vacuolation of podocytes. (Book p784)

questions.q: Match each Fabry investigation with its finding — 1) Urine  2) Renal biopsy … A) Vacuolation of podocytes  B) Maltese cross deposits under polarised light
questions.exp: Fabry disease: urine shows maltese cross deposits under polarised light; renal biopsy shows vacuolation of podocytes (figure 'Fabry's disease'). (Book p784)

questions.q: Fill up: The lipid deposits in the urine of Fabry disease appear as ______ crosses under polarised light.
questions.exp: Urine in Fabry disease: maltese cross deposits under polarised light, from lipid-laden cells. (Book p784)

questions.q: A young man with Fabry disease has both renal and extrarenal disease. Which extrarenal symptom is listed first among his features?
questions.exp: The features list of Fabry disease begins with acroparesthesia, then angiokeratoma (2nd decade), vessel accumulation in heart/cerebrovascular/cornea, and renal involvement. (Book p784)

questions.q: Fabry disease is inherited in an X-linked manner and is a lysosomal storage disorder.
opts: True, but it is a peroxisomal disorder
questions.exp: Fabry disease: X-linked lysosomal storage disease due to α-galactosidase defect. (Book p784)

questions.q: Nail-patella syndrome is inherited as and caused by:
questions.exp: Nail-patella syndrome: AD, LMX1B mutation. (Book p785)

questions.q: Match the nail-patella syndrome features — 1) Nails  2) Knee  3) Pelvis X-ray  4) Renal … A) Iliac horn  B) Dystrophic nails  C) Absent patella  D) Adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria, usually benign
questions.exp: Clinical features of nail-patella syndrome: dystrophic nails, absent patella, iliac horn, and renal manifestation — adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria that is benign (rarely progresses to ESRD). (Book p785)

questions.q: A 16-year-old has microhaematuria and mild proteinuria with absent patellae and dystrophic nails. A pelvic radiograph shows an iliac horn. The renal prognosis is:
opts: Benign — it rarely progresses to ESRD
Rapidly progressive to ESRD within weeks
questions.exp: Renal manifestation of nail-patella syndrome: adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria, benign, rarely progressing to ESRD. (Book p785)

questions.q: Fill up: On X-ray, nail-patella syndrome shows an iliac ______.
questions.exp: Nail-patella syndrome features include the iliac horn, shown in the pelvic radiograph labelled 'iliac horns'. (Book p785)

questions.q: The investigation finding on electron microscopy in nail-patella syndrome is:
questions.exp: Investigation in nail-patella syndrome: EM shows a moth-eaten appearance (figure 'moth eaten appearance'). (Book p785)

questions.q: Match each familial glomerular syndrome with its electron-microscopy signature — 1) Alport syndrome  2) Thin GBM disease  3) Nail-patella syndrome … A) Moth-eaten appearance  B) Splitting + lamellation of lamina densa (basket weave)  C) Uniformly thin basement membrane (<200–300 nm)
questions.exp: EM signatures: Alport → splitting/lamellation of the lamina densa with basket-weave and alternate thick/thin foci; thin GBM disease → uniformly thin (<200–300 nm); nail-patella → moth-eaten appearance. (Book p785)

questions.q: Dystrophic nails and an absent patella are clinical features of nail-patella syndrome along with an iliac horn.
opts: False — dystrophic nails belong to Alport syndrome
False — the absent patella is seen in Fabry disease
True, but the iliac horn occurs only in Alport syndrome
questions.exp: Nail-patella syndrome features: dystrophic nails, absent patella, iliac horn and renal (adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria, benign). (Book p785)

questions.q: Nail-patella syndrome's renal involvement (adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria) is classified as:
opts: Nephrotic — progresses in all cases by 5 years
questions.exp: Renal manifestation of nail-patella syndrome: adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria — benign (rarely progress to ESRD). (Book p785)

questions.q: All but one of the following belong to nail-patella syndrome. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Anterior lenticonus is the pathognomonic ocular sign of Alport syndrome; nail-patella syndrome shows dystrophic nails, absent patella, iliac horn and benign renal involvement. (Book p785)

units.title: Alport syndrome: collagen, inheritance, timeline and eye signs
units.guide: Alport (hereditary) nephritis = COL4A5 mutation, commonest a deletion. Type IV collagen trimers and where each is seen; inheritance 80% X-linked (α5; ESRD by 30 years in males, females carriers), 15% AR and 5% AD (α3/α4; AR ESRD by 40 years, AD mild). Clinical timeline 5→30 years ending in ESRD, with SNHL (low → high frequency) and anterior lenticonus with an oil droplet sign.

units.title: Alport electron microscopy, transplant risk & thin GBM disease
units.guide: LM and IF are normal in Alport syndrome; EM shows splitting/lamellation of the lamina densa with alternating thick and thin foci (basket weave). Treatment is transplant, with a 5% post-transplant risk of Goodpasture syndrome from antibody against α3. Thin GBM disease is AD (COL4A4/A3) with microhaematuria before 5 years, good prognosis and a uniformly thin basement membrane (<200–300 nm).

units.title: Fabry disease: extrarenal signs and renal involvement
units.guide: X-linked lysosomal storage disease (defective α-galactosidase): acroparesthesia, angiokeratoma in the 2nd decade, accumulation in vessels of heart, cerebrovascular system and cornea verticillata, with renal asymptomatic microhaematuria + proteinuria as the earliest feature and ESRD by the 4th–5th decade. Urine maltese cross deposits under polarised light; biopsy shows vacuolation of podocytes.

units.title: Nail-patella syndrome
units.guide: AD disease due to LMX1B mutation: dystrophic nails, absent patella, iliac horn on X-ray, and adolescent microhaematuria + proteinuria that is benign (rarely progressing to ESRD). Electron microscopy gives the moth-eaten appearance, distinct from the Alport basket-weave and the uniformly thin basement membrane of thin GBM disease.
